{{Short description|Family of cubic graphs formed from regular and star polygons}}
[[File:Dürer graph.svg|thumb|The [[Dürer graph]] {{math|''G''(6, 2)}}.]]

In [[graph theory]], the '''generalized Petersen graphs''' are a family of [[cubic graph]]s formed by connecting the vertices of a [[regular polygon]] to the corresponding vertices of a [[star polygon]]. They include the [[Petersen graph]] and generalize one of the ways of constructing the Petersen graph. The generalized Petersen graph family was introduced in 1950 by [[H. S. M. Coxeter]]<ref>{{citation | last = Coxeter | first = H. S. M. | author-link = Harold Scott MacDonald Coxeter | doi = 10.1090/S0002-9904-1950-09407-5 | journal = [[Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society]] | pages = 413–455 | title = Self-dual configurations and regular graphs | volume = 56 | issue = 5 | year = 1950| doi-access = free }}.</ref> and was given its name in 1969 by Mark Watkins.<ref>{{citation | last = Watkins | first = Mark E. | doi = 10.1016/S0021-9800(69)80116-X | journal = [[Journal of Combinatorial Theory]] | pages = 152–164 | title = A Theorem on Tait Colorings with an Application to the Generalized Petersen Graphs | volume = 6| issue = 2 | year = 1969| doi-access = free }}.</ref>

==Definition and notation==
In Watkins' notation, <math>G(n,k)</math> is a graph with vertex set
<math display=block>\{u_0, u_1, \ldots, u_{n-1}, v_0, v_1, \ldots, v_{n-1}\}</math>
and edge set
<math display=block>\{u_iu_{i+1}, u_iv_i, v_iv_{i+k} \mid 0 \le i \le n-1 \}</math>
where subscripts are to be read modulo <math>n</math> and where <math>k<n/2</math>. Some authors use the notation <math>GPG(n,k)</math>. Coxeter's notation for the same graph would be <math>\{n\}+\{n/k\}</math>, a combination of the [[Schläfli symbol]]s for the [[regular polygon|regular {{mvar|n}}-gon]] and [[star polygon]] from which the graph is formed. The Petersen graph itself is <math>G(5,2)</math> or <math>\{5\}+\{5/2\}</math>. Some authors also allow <math>k=n/2</math>, producing a graph that is not a [[regular graph]].<ref name=alspach83/>

Any generalized Petersen graph can also be constructed from a [[voltage graph]] with two vertices, two self-loops, and one other edge.<ref>{{citation | last1 = Gross | first1 = Jonathan L. | last2 = Tucker | first2 = Thomas W. | location = New York | publisher = Wiley | title = Topological Graph Theory | year = 1987}}. Example 2.1.2, p.58.</ref>

==Examples==
Among the generalized Petersen graphs are the <math>n</math>-prism <math>G(n,1)</math>, the [[Dürer graph]] <math>G(6,2)</math>, the [[Möbius-Kantor graph]] <math>G(8,3)</math>, the [[Regular dodecahedron|dodecahedron]] <math>G(10,2)</math>, the [[Desargues graph]] <math>G(10,3)</math> and the [[Nauru graph]] <math>G(12,5)</math>.

Four generalized Petersen graphs – the 3-prism, the 5-prism, the Dürer graph, and <math>G(7,2)</math> – are among the seven graphs that are [[cubic graph|cubic]], [[k-vertex-connected graph|3-vertex-connected]], and [[well-covered graph|well-covered]] (meaning that all of their [[maximal independent set]]s have equal size).<ref>{{citation | last1 = Campbell | first1 = S. R. | last2 = Ellingham | first2 = M. N. | author2-link = Mark Ellingham | last3 = Royle | first3 = Gordon F. | author3-link = Gordon Royle | journal = Journal of Combinatorial Mathematics and Combinatorial Computing | mr = 1220613 | pages = 193–212 | title = A characterisation of well-covered cubic graphs | volume = 13 | year = 1993}}.</ref>

==Properties==
[[File:Generalized Petersen 9 2 Hamiltonicity.svg|thumb|One of the three Hamiltonian cycles in ''G''(9, 2). The other two Hamiltonian cycles in the same graph are symmetric under 40° rotations of the drawing.]]

This family of graphs possesses a number of interesting properties. For example:

* <math>G(n,k)</math> is [[Vertex-transitive graph|vertex-transitive]] (meaning that it has symmetries that take any vertex to any other vertex) if and only if <math>(n,k)=(10,2)</math> or <math>k^2\equiv\pm1\ (\mathrm{mod}\ n)</math>.
* <math>G(n,k)</math> is [[Edge-transitive graph|edge-transitive]] (having symmetries that take any edge to any other edge) only in the following seven cases: <math>(n,k)</math> is {{nowrap|(4, 1)}}, {{nowrap|(5, 2)}}, {{nowrap|(8, 3)}}, {{nowrap|(10, 2)}}, {{nowrap|(10, 3)}}, {{nowrap|(12, 5)}}, {{nowrap|or (24, 5).<ref>{{citation | last1 = Frucht | first1 = R. | author1-link = R. Frucht | last2 = Graver | first2 = J. E. | last3 = Watkins | first3 = M. E. | doi = 10.1017/S0305004100049811 | journal = Proceedings of the Cambridge Philosophical Society | pages = 211–218 | title = The groups of the generalized Petersen graphs | volume = 70 | issue = 2 | year = 1971 | bibcode = 1971PCPS...70..211F }}.</ref>}} These seven graphs are therefore the only [[symmetric graph|symmetric]] generalized Petersen graphs.
* <math>G(n,k)</math> is [[bipartite graph|bipartite]] if and only if <math>n</math> is even and <math>k</math> is odd.
* <math>G(n,k)</math> is a [[Cayley graph]] if and only if <math>k^2\equiv 1\ (\mathrm{mod}\ n)</math>.
* <math>G(n,k)</math> is [[hypohamiltonian graph|hypohamiltonian]] when <math>n</math> is congruent to 5 modulo 6 and <math>k</math> is 2, <math>n-2</math>, or <math>(n\pm1)/2</math> (these four choices of ''k'' lead to isomorphic graphs). It is also non-[[hamiltonian graph|Hamiltonian]] when <math>n</math> is divisible by 4, at least equal to 8, and <math>k=n/2</math>. In all other cases it has a [[Hamiltonian cycle]].<ref name=alspach83>{{citation | last = Alspach | first = B. R. | authorlink = Brian Alspach | doi = 10.1016/0095-8956(83)90042-4 | mr = 0714452 | journal = [[Journal of Combinatorial Theory]] | series=Series B | pages = 293–312 | title = The classification of Hamiltonian generalized Petersen graphs | volume = 34 | issue = 3 | year = 1983| doi-access = free }}.</ref> When <math>n</math> is congruent to 3 modulo&nbsp;6, <math>G(n,2)</math> has exactly three Hamiltonian cycles.<ref>{{citation|title=Cubic graphs with three Hamiltonian cycles are not always uniquely edge colorable|first=Andrew|last=Thomason|doi=10.1002/jgt.3190060218|journal=[[Journal of Graph Theory]]| volume=6 |issue=2 |year=1982|pages=219–221}}.</ref> For <math>G(n,2)</math>, the number of Hamiltonian cycles can be computed by a formula that depends on the congruence class of <math>n</math> modulo 6 and involves the [[Fibonacci number]]s.<ref>{{citation | last = Schwenk | first = Allen J. | doi = 10.1016/0095-8956(89)90064-6 | issue = 1 | journal = [[Journal of Combinatorial Theory]] | series = Series B | mr = 1007713 | pages = 53–59 | title = Enumeration of Hamiltonian cycles in certain generalized Petersen graphs | volume = 47 | year = 1989| doi-access = free }}.</ref> Linear recurrence relations for the number of Hamiltonian cycles have also been found for <math>G(n,3)</math> and <math>G(n,4)</math>.<ref>{{citation|last = Haugland|first = Jan K.|doi = 10.61091/jcmcc126-18|volume = 126|journal = J. Combin. Math. Combin. Comput.|year = 2025|pages = 263–278|title = On the number of Hamiltonian cycles in the generalized Petersen graph|doi-access = free|arxiv = 2503.08326}}.</ref>
* Every generalized Petersen graph is a [[unit distance graph]].<ref>{{citation | last1 = Žitnik | first1 = Arjana | last2 = Horvat | first2 = Boris | last3 = Pisanski | first3 = Tomaž | author3-link = Tomaž Pisanski | series = IMFM preprints | title = All generalized Petersen graphs are unit-distance graphs | url = http://preprinti.imfm.si/PDF/01109.pdf | volume = 1109 | year = 2010 | access-date = 2017-04-07 | archive-date = 2018-07-24 | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20180724094410/http://preprinti.imfm.si/PDF/01109.pdf | url-status = dead }}.</ref>

===Isomorphisms===
<math>G(n,k)</math> is isomorphic to <math>G(n,\ell)</math> if and only if <math>k\equiv\pm\ell\ (\mathrm{mod}\ n)</math> or <math>k\ell\equiv\pm1\ (\mathrm{mod}\ n)</math>.<ref>{{citation|title=The isomorphism classes of the generalized Petersen graphs|first1=Alice|last1=Steimle| first2=William|last2=Staton|journal=[[Discrete Mathematics (journal)|Discrete Mathematics]]| volume=309| issue=1 |year=2009 |pages=231–237 |doi=10.1016/j.disc.2007.12.074 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

===Girth===
The [[girth (graph theory)|girth]] of <math>G(n,k)</math> is at least 3 and at most 8, in particular:<ref name="FH">{{Citation | url= http://danielaferrero.wp.txstate.edu/files/2015/03/Component-connectivity-generalized-Petersen-graphs.pdf | doi= 10.1080/00207160.2013.878023 | journal= International Journal of Computer Mathematics | first1=Daniela | last1=Ferrero |author1-link=Daniela Ferrero| first2=Sarah | last2=Hanusch | pages=1940–1963 | volume=91 | issue=9 | year=2014 | title=Component connectivity of generalized Petersen graphs | issn=0020-7160 | access-date=2018-10-20 | archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20181020182041/http://danielaferrero.wp.txstate.edu/files/2015/03/Component-connectivity-generalized-Petersen-graphs.pdf | archive-date=2018-10-20 | url-status=dead }}</ref>

:<math>g(G(n,k)) \le \min \left \{8,k+3,\frac{n}{\gcd(n,k)} \right \}.</math>

===Chromatic number and chromatic index===
Generalized Petersen graphs are [[regular graph]]s of [[Degree (graph theory)|degree]] three, so according to [[Brooks' theorem]] their chromatic number can only be two or three. More exactly:

:<math>\chi(G(n,k))= \begin{cases}
  2 & 2 \mid n \land 2 \nmid k \\
  3 & 2 \nmid n \lor 2 \mid k \\
\end{cases}</math>

Where <math>\land</math> denotes the logical [[Logical conjunction|AND]], while <math>\lor</math> the logical [[Logical disjunction|OR]]. Here, <math>\mid</math> denotes divisibility, and <math>\nmid</math> denotes its negation. For example, the chromatic number of <math>G(5,2)</math> is 3.

<gallery>
Petersen_graph_3-coloring.svg|A 3-coloring of the [[Petersen graph]] or <math>G(5,2)</math>
Desargues graph 2COL.svg|A 2-coloring of the [[Desargues graph]] or <math>G(10,3)</math>
Dürer graph 3COL.svg|A 3-coloring of the [[Dürer graph]] or <math>G(6,2)</math>
</gallery>

The [[Petersen graph]], being a [[Snark (graph theory)|snark]], has a [[chromatic index]] of 4: its edges require four colors. All other generalized Petersen graphs have chromatic index 3. These are the only possibilities, by [[Vizing's theorem]].<ref>{{citation | last1 = Castagna | first1 = Frank | last2 = Prins | first2 = Geert Caleb Ernst | journal = Pacific Journal of Mathematics | title = Every generalized Petersen graph has a Tait coloring | volume = 40 | issue = 1 | pages = 53–58 | year = 1972 | doi = 10.2140/pjm.1972.40.53|issn=0030-8730|mr=304223|zbl=0236.05106| doi-access = free}}</ref>

The generalized Petersen graph <math>G(9,2)</math> is one of the few graphs known to have [[Uniquely colorable graph#Unique edge colorability|only one 3-edge-coloring]].<ref>{{citation|first=Béla|last=Bollobás|authorlink=Béla Bollobás|title=Extremal Graph Theory|publisher=Dover|year=2004|page=233}}. Reprint of 1978 Academic Press edition.</ref>

<gallery>
PetersenBarveniHran.svg|A 4-edge-coloring of the [[Petersen graph]] or <math>G(5,2)</math>
Dürer graph 3color edge.svg|A 3-edge-coloring of the [[Dürer graph]] or <math>G(6,2)</math>
3-colored dodecahedron.svg|A 3-edge-coloring of the [[dodecahedron]] or <math>G(10,2)</math>
Desargues graph 3color edge.svg|A 3-edge-coloring of the [[Desargues graph]] or <math>G(10,3)</math>
Symmetric group 4; Cayley graph 1,5,21 (Nauru Petersen); matrices.svg|A 3-edge-coloring of the [[Nauru graph]] or <math>G(12,5)</math>
</gallery>

The Petersen graph itself is the only generalized Petersen graph that is not 3-[[edge coloring|edge-colorable]].<ref>{{citation | last1 = Castagna | first1 = Frank | last2 = Prins | first2 = Geert | journal = [[Pacific Journal of Mathematics]] | title = Every Generalized Petersen Graph has a Tait Coloring | volume = 40 | pages = 53–58 | year = 1972 | doi = 10.2140/pjm.1972.40.53 | doi-access = free }}.</ref>
